name: Collecting Emissions Data
title: Collecting Emissions Data
answer: Collecting emissions data means gathering primary activity data and emission factors across scope 1, scope 2, and scope 3 categories for an organization or portfolio. It covers direct fuel combustion, purchased electricity and heat, and upstream and downstream value chain activities such as business travel, purchased goods, and use of sold products. The practice includes both measured data from meters and sensors and estimated data from spend, activity, or production proxies. It is the input layer for carbon accounting, reporting, and target setting.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Collecting emissions data means gathering primary activity data and emission factors across scope 1, scope 2, and scope 3 categories for an organization or portfolio. It covers direct fuel combustion, purchased electricity and heat, and upstream and downstream value chain activities such as business travel, purchased goods, and use of sold products. The practice includes both measured data from meters and sensors and estimated data from spend, activity, or production proxies. It is the input layer for carbon accounting, reporting, and target setting.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of utility billing portals, building management systems, fleet telematics, supplier surveys, and enterprise resource planning systems. Data is typically consolidated in cloud databases or carbon accounting platforms that store activity records, emission factor libraries, and audit logs. Many teams use spreadsheets as an interim layer before moving data into a structured system. Application programming interfaces connect utility data aggregators and financial systems to the emissions repository.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners map emission sources to an inventory boundary, then collect activity data for each source and multiply it by an appropriate emission factor. For missing data, they apply extrapolation, proxy data, or spend based factors, and they document the estimation method. Quality checks compare current period data against prior periods and against physical plausibility ranges. The result is a reconciled dataset with source, unit, factor, and calculation traceability.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Emissions data carries risks around accuracy, completeness, and double counting, especially when supplier or customer data is reused across organizations. Provenance requires recording who supplied each data point, when it was collected, and what conversion or allocation was applied. Access controls separate raw activity data from reported totals, and versioning preserves the dataset used for each disclosure. Regulatory regimes may require third party assurance over data collection and calculation processes.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Collection is moving toward automated meter reads, supplier specific factors, and continuous data feeds rather than annual manual surveys. Machine learning is being used to classify spend categories, detect outliers, and fill gaps in supplier reported data. The direction is toward auditable, real time inventories that can support internal carbon pricing and product level footprints. Standard setters are pushing for more primary data and less reliance on industry average factors.
